level_1_heading: Docling: An Efficient Open-Source Toolkit for AI-driven Document Conversion
chunk_text: We introduce Docling, an easy-to-use, self-contained, MIT-licensed, open-source toolkit for document conversion that can parse several types of popular document formats into a unified, richly structured representation. It is powered by state-of-the-art specialized AI models for layout analysis (DocLayNet) and table structure recognition (TableFormer), and runs efficiently on commodity hardware in a small resource budget. Docling is released as a Python package and can be used as a Python API or as a CLI tool. Docling's modular architecture and efficient document representation make it easy to implement extensions, new features, models, and customizations. Docling has been integrated in other popular open-source frameworks (e.g., LangChain, LlamaIndex, spaCy), making it a natural fit for processing documents and developing high-end applications. The open-source community has engaged actively, gathering 10k stars on GitHub in less than a month and ranking as the No. 1 trending repository worldwide in November 2024. Docling parses common document formats (PDF, Images, MS Office formats, HTML) and exports to Markdown, JSON, and HTML; applies advanced AI for document understanding including detailed page layout, OCR, reading order, figure extraction, and table structure recognition; establishes a unified DoclingDocument data model for rich document representation and operations; provides fully local execution capabilities suitable for sensitive data and air-gapped environments; has an ecosystem of plug-and-play integrations with generative AI frameworks including LangChain and LlamaIndex; and can leverage hardware accelerators such as GPUs.

metadata.level_1_heading: Docling: An Efficient Open-Source Toolkit for AI-driven Document Conversion

level_1_heading: Docling: An Efficient Open-Source Toolkit for AI-driven Document Conversion
chunk_text: Docling v2 introduces a unified document representation, DoclingDocument, a Pydantic data model that can express various common document features such as text, tables, pictures, captions, lists, and more; document hierarchy with sections and groups; disambiguation between main body and headers, footers (furniture); layout information (bounding boxes) for all items if available; and provenance information such as page numbers and document origin. This data model enables representing document content in a unified manner regardless of the source document format. The DoclingDocument class defines APIs for document construction, inspection, and export. Users can incrementally build a DoclingDocument, traverse its contents in reading order, or export to commonly used formats. Docling supports lossless serialization to and deserialization from JSON, and lossy export formats such as Markdown and HTML, which cannot retain all meta information. A DoclingDocument can be passed to a chunker class abstraction that returns a stream of chunks, each capturing some part of the document as a string with metadata. Docling defines a chunker class hierarchy allowing downstream applications to leverage popular frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex for flexible chunking approaches.

level_1_heading: Docling: An Efficient Open-Source Toolkit for AI-driven Document Conversion
chunk_text: Document formats are broadly categorized into two types: low-level formats like PDF files or scanned images, which encode the visual representation of the document and require recovery of semantics through AI methods such as OCR, layout analysis, or table structure recognition; and markup-based formats including MS Office, HTML, Markdown, and others, which preserve semantic content and are comparatively easier to parse. Docling implements several parser backends to read and interpret different formats and routes their output to a fitting processing pipeline. For PDFs, Docling provides backends that retrieve all text content and geometric properties and render the visual representation of each page. For markup-based formats, the backends create a DoclingDocument representation directly. Some formats provide element locations and page provenance, others do not. DoclingDocument data model handles both cases. Due to limitations and restrictive licensing of existing open-source PDF parsing libraries, Docling developed a custom PDF parser based on the low-level qpdf library, available as a separate package docling-parse and the default PDF backend. An alternative PDF backend using pypdfium is also provided. For markup-based formats like HTML, Markdown, MS Office (Word, PowerPoint, Excel), and plain formats like AsciiDoc, Docling uses third-party parsing libraries such as BeautifulSoup, Marko, python-docx, python-pptx, and openpyxl, extracting common document elements and reflecting correct hierarchy levels.

level_1_heading: Docling: An Efficient Open-Source Toolkit for AI-driven Document Conversion
chunk_text: Pipelines in Docling serve as an orchestration layer which iterates through documents, gathers extracted data from a parser backend, and applies a chain of models to build and enrich the DoclingDocument representation. Docling provides two standard pipelines: the StandardPdfPipeline, which leverages state-of-the-art AI models to reconstruct a high-quality DoclingDocument from PDF or image input; and the SimplePipeline, which handles all markup-based formats and may apply further enrichment models. Pipelines can be fully customized by subclassing or cloning the default pipeline, allowing users to customize model chains, add or replace models, and introduce additional configuration parameters. Custom pipelines can be provided as arguments to the main document conversion API.

level_1_heading: Docling: An Efficient Open-Source Toolkit for AI-driven Document Conversion
chunk_text: Docling releases two highly capable AI models: a layout analysis model (DocLayNet) which is an accurate object detector for page elements, and TableFormer, a state-of-the-art table structure recognition model. The layout analysis model predicts bounding boxes and classes of various elements on a page, trained on a human-annotated dataset. The TableFormer model predicts logical row and column structure of tables, determining which cells belong to headers or body, handling complex table characteristics such as partial or no borderlines, empty cells, cell spans, and inconsistent indentation or alignment. The PDF pipeline feeds all detected table objects from layout analysis to TableFormer by providing an image crop of the table and included text cells. TableFormer predictions are matched back to PDF cells during post-processing to avoid expensive re-transcription of the table image crop. Docling uses the Hugging Face transformers library and Safetensors file format for layout analysis. The PDF parser is custom-built based on qpdf to overcome limitations of existing open-source PDF parsing libraries.

level_1_heading: Docling: An Efficient Open-Source Toolkit for AI-driven Document Conversion
chunk_text: Docling utilizes OCR to convert scanned PDFs and extract content from embedded bitmap images. It integrates with EasyOCR, a popular third-party OCR library supporting many languages, and Tesseract as an alternative. EasyOCR provides reasonable transcription quality but runs fairly slow on CPU, making it the biggest compute expense in the pipeline. In the final pipeline stage, Docling assembles all prediction results from each page into the DoclingDocument representation, as defined in the auxiliary Python package docling-core. The generated document object is passed through a post-processing model which leverages algorithms to augment features such as correcting reading order or matching figures with captions.

level_1_heading: Docling: An Efficient Open-Source Toolkit for AI-driven Document Conversion
chunk_text: We implemented several measures to enable a fair and reproducible benchmark across all tested assets. Specifically, the experimental setup accounts for the following factors: All assets are installed in the latest available versions, in a clean Python environment, and configured to use state-of-the-art processing options and models where applicable. Non-essential functionalities were selectively disabled to achieve a compatible feature-set across all compared libraries. When running experiments on CPU, all assets are informed to use a CPU thread budget of 8 threads via the OMP_NUM_THREADS environment variable and accepted configuration options. The L4 GPU on our AWS EC2 VM is hidden. When running experiments on the L4 GPU, CUDA acceleration is enabled in all accepted configuration options, ensuring the GPU is visible and all required runtimes for AI inference are installed with CUDA support.

chunk_text: Figure 3 shows the distribution of conversion times for all documents ordered by number of pages, across all system configurations (x86 CPU, M3 Max, L4 GPU). The relationship between document length and conversion time is not strictly linear due to varying frequency of tables and bitmap elements requiring OCR or table structure recognition. Processing a page requires between 0.6 seconds (5th percentile) and 16.3 seconds (95th percentile), with a median of 0.79 seconds on x86 CPU. On M3 Max SoC, median times are 0.26/0.32/6.48 seconds per page (.05/median/.95), and on Nvidia L4 GPU 57/114/2081 milliseconds per page. Disabling OCR saves 60% runtime on x86 CPU and M3 Max SoC, 50% on L4 GPU. Disabling table structure recognition saves 16% on x86 CPU and M3 Max SoC, 24% on L4 GPU. Disabling both OCR and table structure recognition saves around 75% runtime on all systems.

level_3_heading: Profiling Docling's AI Pipeline and Comparison to Other Tools
chunk_text: Profiling Docling's PDF backend and AI models shows OCR is the most expensive operation, engaging in 578 pages in the benchmark dataset. Transcribing a page with EasyOCR takes 1.6s on L4 GPU, 13s on x86 CPU, and 5s on M3 Max SoC. The layout model spends 44ms on L4 GPU, 633ms on x86 CPU, and 271ms on M3 Max SoC per page. TableFormer spends 400ms on L4 GPU, 1.74s on x86 CPU, and 704ms on M3 Max SoC per table. TableFormer had less impact than other AI models since tables appeared on only 28% of pages. Parsing a PDF page took 81ms on x86 CPU and 44ms on M3 Max SoC (no GPU support). Comparison to other tools (Marker, MinerU, Unstructured) shows Docling leads without GPU support with 3.1 sec/page on x86 CPU and 1.27 sec/page on M3 Max SoC. MinerU leads with CUDA acceleration on Nvidia L4 GPU at 0.21 sec/page. Unstructured does not benefit from GPU acceleration.

chunk_text: Docling is evolving into a mainstream package for document conversion with support for PDF, MS Office formats, images, HTML, and more, making it a universal choice for downstream applications. Docling's modular architecture allows easy extension of the model library and pipelines. Planned future extensions include a figure-classifier model, an equation-recognition model, and a code-recognition model to improve conversion quality and augment extracted metadata. An open-source quality evaluation framework will be developed for tasks like layout analysis, table structure recognition, reading order detection, and text transcription, enabling transparent quality comparisons based on public benchmarks such as DP-Bench and OmniDocBench. The Docling codebase is open under the MIT license. The roadmap and discussion are available on the GitHub repository, encouraging community contributions and improvements.
